articles.title: Spot the conversation hogger – and do something about it | Letter
articles.summary: Penelope Mavor suggests that listening is not a passive act, so you could interrupt the flow. These conversational hoggers … don’t they know we were born with two ears and one mouth for a reason?
body: It is an interesting reflection to see which of the five hoggers more frequently turn up in our own lives. As a people pleaser and introvert, I have a track record of meeting many monologuists. I pretend to listen, but secretly resent them and their audacity. I just want them to ask about me.

I have learned that although interruption can feel violent, sometimes it is a courageous act. When the speaker has just lost connection with the audience and themselves, we have to bring them back. That is what I loved most about the article – it reminded us that we do have options. We can start noticing how we turn up. How am I listening and speaking? What is my responsibility here?
A great listener can help to transform the conversation – listening is not a passive act. And in talking, am I actually being interesting? Am I talking as if being listened to?

articles.title: Marks and Spencer’s first LFW catwalk gamble pays off with compelling looks at affordable prices
articles.summary: Retailer’s message is ‘fashion with a small f’ as it picks up on trends and brings styles for everyone to debut runway show. Joan Collins declared the coats “very chic”, and has her eye on a graceful ivory evening dress with caped shoulders.
body: The show, held at the Design Museum for 310 guests including Ian Wright and Jamie Carragher, was a gamble on both sides. Would snobby fashionistas be traumatised by elasticated waistbands and practical rainwear? Would M&S customers be alienated by a world of £2,000 handbags and shoes you can’t walk in?

The style message was “fashion with a small f, not a capital F”, said the M&S womenswear director, Maddy Evans. The look was new enough to be compelling (sharp kilts instead of flouncy tiered skirts, low-rise slouchy denim replacing mom jeans), but pitched at a before-the-watershed comfort level. A judicious amount of catwalk theatre was added with some sauce (a very short skirt, the odd semi-visible nipple) and a little zeitgeisty styling (faux fur stoles, Charli xcx-adjacent sunglasses).

The real stunner is the price. All the clothes in this collection went on sale as the show began on Friday, with half of the pieces under £50. The most expensive, a leather coat, will retail for £450. The message – that catwalk style is for everyone – is a win for London fashion week, which has struggled to feel relevant to real lives as designer prices have soared during a cost of living crisis.

articles.title: ‘A critical moment’: concern UK is not up to speed in acting on AI risks
articles.summary: Andy Burnham’s focus on immediate domestic problems leads some to fear issue has dropped off government’s radar. Towards the end of Keir Starmer’s time in office, his senior ministers, alarmed by the latest developments in artificial intelligence, began drawing up plans for a new AI safety law.
body: They ordered a review of existing legislation to see what powers they already had, according to those briefed on the plans, and were exploring whether they could force the world’s most advanced technology companies to submit their products for safety testing before launching them.
In the midst of the political chaos that engulfed the former prime minister as he fought to remain in office, however, the plans fell by the wayside.

Now, after two weeks in which the world has been told there is a greater than 10% chance the technology could “kill all humans”, and King Charles has warned about its potentially destructive capabilities, the government’s attention has turned again to what to do about AI.

Andy Burnham, Starmer’s successor in Downing Street, has said relatively little about the technology in the past, and in one of his first acts in office he scrapped the department that had been leading the legislative work.

articles.title: BrewDog creditors owed £190m will not be paid in full, say administrators
articles.summary: There are ‘insufficient funds’ to pay unpaid wages, tax owed to HMRC and overdue bills, accountants say. Accountants picking over the remains of BrewDog, the “punk” beer company that collapsed earlier this year, have said that creditors who are owed about £190m will not be paid back.
body: In an update on their progress, administrators at AlixPartners warned there were “insufficient funds” to pay debts in full related to unpaid wages, tax owed to HM Revenue and Customs, and overdue bills from other businesses.

Earlier this year, the US cannabis and drinks company Tilray snapped up BrewDog’s brand, intellectual property, UK breweries and 11 bars in a rescue deal for about £33m, agreed after the brewer fell into administration.
But the deal in March did not includemost of BrewDog’s chain of bars, with 38 closing and 440 staff losing their jobs.
The collapse rendered worthless the investments of 200,000 “equity punks”, the small investors who crowdfunded the business.

articles.title: 12 Friendsgiving-Friendly Airbnbs to Book If You Want to Be the Martha Stewart of Your Group
articles.summary: Equipped with multiple bedrooms, full kitchens, and grand dining tables, these rentals will help you and your crew celebrate America’s favorite holiday in style.
body: Thanksgiving has taken many forms since its inception in 1621, and if there’s anything the modern portmanteau “Friendsgiving” has taught us, it’s that you don’t need a traditional family to enjoy America’s favorite feast. And I’m here to tell you you don’t need to have the perfect home to host one, either. Thanks to Airbnb, you can simply rent your dream holiday house.

For all you East Coasters, there’s an abundance of country-chic properties nestled in nature just waiting to help foster quality time without the stress—you know, the kinds of sprawling homesteads Martha Stewart would be thrilled to baste a turkey in. The Airbnbs on this list are ideal for a group getaway, equipped with multiple bedrooms, full kitchens (with ovens big enough for your bird), and grand dining tables, so you can whip up Thanksgiving dinner with ease. Some even have game rooms and saunas, perfect for winding down after the big meal.
From lakeside log cabins in New Hampshire to restored farmhouses in the Hudson Valley, these are the best Friendsgiving-friendly Airbnbs on the East Coast, separated by state.

articles.title: How to Spend the Perfect Autumn Day in London
articles.summary: A local's guide to the pastries to indulge in, the galleries to amble around, and the cocktails to sip before supper during what is, arguably, the city's best season.
body: I’m perhaps (okay, most definitely) biased, but I truly believe that London is at its best in the autumn. It’s like the whole city moves at a different pace—energized by the summer we’ve just had and excited for the festivities on the horizon. And then there’s the never-ending list of autumnal activities to enjoy. As someone who creates a new ‘autumn to-do list’ in my notes app each year (if you don’t believe me, just ask my Condé Nast Traveller UK colleagues), I felt it my duty to share my autumn-loving insider knowledge. From morning cinnamon bun to evening martini, here’s how to spend a dreamy fall day in London.

Tell me what could be a more fitting start to the day than a caffeine fix at London’s coziest coffee spot. There’s a real buzz in the air, both from the eager Londoners queuing patiently for their order, and from the heady fumes of roasting beans—piled up like mountains of glossy jewels behind the counter. I love that despite the slight chill in the air, you’ll still find the scant tables and chairs outside absolutely packed with guests, hands wrapped around steaming coffee mugs.

articles.title: A New Generation of Jewelry Designers Is Bringing Back Art Deco
articles.summary: “I’m drawn to Art Deco’s ability to reinterpret ancient references into modern forms,” says 2026 CFDA finalist Julia Ferentinos of Juju Vera.
body: A newfound appreciation for Art Deco’s visual language has resurfaced recently in the jewelry space. The result is a renaissance of decorative flourishes, from ornate drop earrings to tasseled pendant necklaces and gemstone-encrusted collars, which are finding a prominent place in everyday wardrobes as an expression of personal style.

This reawakening can be traced to a new generation of jewelry designers capturing the refined yet opulent nature of the 1920s design movement through a contemporary lens: Brazilian-born fine jewelry designer Fernando Jorge brings architectural Art Deco patterns to life in his Deep Vertex series through geometric structures in onyx, jade, and mother of pearl. Sophie Buhai, too, has become known for her sculptural take on jewelry and functional objects, hand-crafted in recycled silver and semi-precious stones like jade, carnelian, and lapis.

articles.title: A New Museum Show Explores the Sprawling, Multifaceted Work of Tremaine Emory
articles.summary: Designer Tremaine Emory of Denim Tears receives his first solo museum exhibition, exploring the political and cultural messages of his design work.
body: Even before Tremaine Emory had his own label, Denim Tears, his impact on the fashion world loomed large. He has worked with a variety of popular brands—Stüssy, Marc Jacobs, Yeezy—helping to shape their look. And since launching Denim Tears, he has collaborated with brands like Dior, Levi’s, and Ugg, as well as with the artist David Hammons and the late Virgil Abloh. For a short time, he was also the creative director at streetwear brand Supreme.

All the while, Emory has engaged with race and politics in his work. Denim Tears was launched in 2019, 400 years after the first known slaves arrived in America; and its name is rife with meaning: it refers to cotton—the textile around which slavery was built—and the pain and suffering Black people endured to harvest it.
points: Designer Tremaine Emory of Denim Tears receives his first solo museum exhibition, exploring the political and cultural messages of his design work.

articles.title: I Love How Much Tom Cruise Loves Taylor Swift
articles.summary: “She was schooling me on football,” Cruise told Jimmy Fallon of his and Swift's outing to watch the Kansas City Chiefs play the Denver Broncos on Monday.
body: Taylor Swift is no slouch in the “famous friends” department (not for nothing do I still dream of being invited to her one of her old celebrity-studdied Independence Day parties ), but the latest pal that she was spotted watching a football game with wasn’t a fellow pop star or model—it was none other than Tom Cruise.

“She was schooling me on football,” Cruise admitted during an appearance on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon on Thursday, recalling his visit to Arrowhead Stadium on Monday to see Swift’s husband, Travis Kelce, and the rest of the Chiefs take on the Denver Broncos in Kansas City. “She was bringing the football. First of all, she’s a genius. I’ve been following her since she was a kid. Everybody there, all their friends…they’re a beautiful couple and magical in their own right.”
And he went on! “She’s funny. She’s got such a great sense of humor. A brilliant writer, also. Brilliant musician, director, very skilled…” I mean, Cruise does famously love to emote, but I agree!

articles.title: Why I’m Officially Done Trying to “Find Myself” on Vacation
articles.summary: Somewhere along the line, a simple holiday stopped being enough. We argue it’s time to abandon the self-improvement treadmill while away and enjoy the view.
body: I am lying on a massage table somewhere far, far away. Two horses hover beside me. A woman speaks to me in tongues while performing reiki. I am subsequently bidden to release my ancestral trauma by setting fire to some crumpled paper in a bowl. I do so with gusto. I shall be transformed.

I carry this gleeful, hopeful sentiment within me on the plane home. I feel light and free; my heart is filled with hope. But the very next day I suffered a monumental insult from someone I considered a friend. Three months on, I’m just as skint and single as I ever was—and my gym body hasn’t arrived either. As I stare down the barrel of the Piccadilly line tunnel at Covent Garden for the 8,000th time, it appears my requested manifestations haven’t arrived on cue. Given the retreat carried a $25,000-odd price tag, I’d have expected the universe to put me in the skip-the-queue line for psychic fulfilment.

I’m not alone in hoping for something to change post-holiday. Many of us buy into the idea of a break away as a total reset, a chance to usher in a new iteration of ourselves. It’s a cliché that young people head off to “find themselves” on a gap year for a reason.
